title: The trade-off hiding inside a memory-mapped file (mmap) used for high-throughput write-ahead logging
spec: Explain what a memory-mapped file (mmap) used for high-throughput write-ahead logging gives up in order to be good at what it is good at. A sudden kernel page flush block stalls application threads waiting on synchronous I/O. Success: states both sides of the trade and says who notices the side that was given up.
result: A memorymapped file for highthroughput writeahead logging trades strict durability and ordering guarantees for speed: the kernel can keep dirty pages in RAM and batch their flushes, so writes appear almost instantly to the application. The price paid is that the application loses immediate visibility of when data is actually on stable storage, and any sudden kernelinitiated pageflush (e.g., due to memory pressure) can block the thread that performed a synchronousfsync or msync. The side that notices the loss is the application (or its users), which experiences latency spikes or stalls when the kernel finally forces the pending pages to disk.

title: Hardening a systemd unit with no restart limit against denial of service
spec: Identify how an attacker can exhaust resources via a systemd unit with no restart limit and the mitigation mechanism to limit amplification. A crash-looped service restarts infinitely and the machine burns CPU on a service that can never start. Success: names one resource exhaustion vector and one rate-limiting or quota rule.
result: An attacker can trigger repeated service failures, causing systemd to start and stop the unit indefinitely. This can exhaust CPU through process creation and teardown, and may also fill journal or system logs with repeated failure messages. Apply systemd’s start-rate limiting with `StartLimitIntervalSec=` and `StartLimitBurst=` in the unit’s `[Unit]` section—for example, `StartLimitIntervalSec=60s` and `StartLimitBurst=5`. After five failed starts within 60 seconds, systemd refuses further starts until the interval expires. Setting a nonzero `RestartSec=` also reduces restart amplification by adding a delay between attempts.

title: Handling split-brain scenarios in a RocksDB LSM-tree experiencing severe write amplification

title: Hardening a distributed lock with lease renewal failing due to garbage collection pauses against denial of service

result: An attacker can submit a large number of lock-acquisition requests, creating unbounded queued waiters and renewal/retry traffic. title: Default Linux TCP TIME_WAIT duration and its MSL basis
spec: State the RFC 793 Maximum Segment Lifetime and the TIME_WAIT duration a Linux socket holds, and that Linux uses a fixed constant rather than a runtime 2*MSL. Success: gives the TIME_WAIT duration in seconds and the kernel constant that sets it.
result: RFC 793 specifies a Maximum Segment Lifetime (MSL) of 2 minutes (120 seconds). A literal 2×MSL interpretation would therefore imply a 240-second TIME_WAIT period. Linux does not calculate TIME_WAIT from the RFC MSL at runtime. Its TCP implementation uses a fixed kernel constant, `TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN`, defined as `60 * HZ`, so the default TIME_WAIT duration is 60 seconds (subject to the kernel’s timer granularity). Thus, on standard Linux kernels, a closed TCP connection normally remains in TIME_WAIT for approximately 60 seconds, not 2×RFC 793’s 120-second MSL.

The entire system operates as a highcapacity, lowlatency backbone for global internet traffic.

title: Default Linux TCP TIME_WAIT duration and its MSL basis
spec: State the RFC 793 Maximum Segment Lifetime and the TIME_WAIT duration a Linux socket holds, and that Linux uses a fixed constant rather than a runtime 2*MSL. Success: gives the TIME_WAIT duration in seconds and the kernel constant that sets it.
result: RFC 793 defines the Maximum Segment Lifetime (MSL) as 2 minutes. Its traditional TIME_WAIT rule is therefore 2×MSL, or 4 minutes (240 seconds). This results in an effective TIME_WAIT duration of 60 seconds, assuming normal kernel timer behavior, rather than 240 seconds.
